cue: How do you describe the flutter of nerves before something big?

es.literal: to have butterflies in the stomach
es.meaning: To feel a nervous flutter, usually from excitement or attraction.
es.example: Cada vez que la ve tiene mariposas en el estómago.
es.exampleTranslation: He gets butterflies every time he sees her.

it.literal: to have the butterflies in the stomach
it.meaning: To feel a nervous flutter, usually from excitement or attraction.
it.example: Ogni volta che la vede ha le farfalle nello stomaco.
it.exampleTranslation: He gets butterflies every time he sees her.

bridge.note: These two match because neither of them invented it. Butterflies in the stomach is an English expression that both languages took in during the last century, which is why the images line up perfectly where older shared idioms usually differ by a word or an animal. That makes this a useful thing to notice rather than a coincidence to admire: when two Romance idioms agree exactly, a recent English original is often the reason. What each language did do is its own grammar — Italian takes the definite article, LE farfalle, and folds the preposition into it, NELLO stomaco; Spanish does neither.

interference.es_to_it: Italian wants the article Spanish leaves out — ho LE farfalle nello stomaco — and contracts in + lo into nello, because stomaco takes lo rather than il. 'In il stomaco' is doubly wrong.
interference.it_to_es: Spanish drops the article and keeps the preposition separate: mariposas EN EL estómago, not 'las mariposas'. And Spanish marks the stress — estómago — where Italian does not.

THE ENGLISH-BORROWING CLAIM IS THE BRIDGE AND IT IS UNVERIFIED: I assert both sides are 20th-century calques of the English phrase rather than parallel native developments. It is very likely right — the perfection of the match is itself the evidence — but it is an etymological claim stated as fact to subscribers, so it needs a source or a reviewer's confirmation before approval, not just plausibility. If either language turns out to have an older independent attestation, the whole bridge is wrong.
